title: Cora's Clever Charter Banner
markdown:
Gadzooks, the canals of Oakhaven were singing again. Reeds took the secrets and kept them wet. Boats slept like water dragons with their sails furled, and the Grand Book Festival filled the air with old paper, ink, and damp earth. For Cora the deer, apprentice tailor to Master Hemlock, it was also the season of mild mayhem: a dropped stitch, a crooked seam, a frayed hem waiting just offstage.

Her days were measuring and pinning. Her rival, Elara, a swan tailor whose glide never ruffled, never frayed, never looked flustered. Cora wanted to stomp. She pored over diagrams until her brow ached, and still her stitches came a fraction loose or a whisker tight. Vexing did not cover it.

This year’s festival had drawn authors from far towns, illustrators whose creatures seemed ready to step off paper, and a hushed throng of readers who treated bookmarks like passports. Stalls sold toasted chestnuts and ink-stained bookmarks. A string quartet argued politely with a concertina. Cora’s assigned cake-walk was the collar of a famous children’s author’s favourite tweed jacket, a garment that had seen more storytimes than most librarians. She practised the delicate seam in her mind while snipping a stray thread, imagining the author’s throat comfortable at last. Then Elara swooped in, not to sabotage, only to mention thread tension, a gentle tilt of the beak making the advice sound inevitable. The suggestion was, infuriatingly, correct. Cora’s ears drooped. She had meant a nuanced give and stretch for comfort, the sort of mercy a collar owes a storyteller. The words would not come. Arguing with Elara felt like arguing with sunshine.

Ned the mole emerged from backstage shadows with dirt on his nose and a moleskin vest that smelled of pine and damp earth. He lived in ropes, pulleys, and the comfort of being useful where the audience never looked. He never judged; he worked. He would fix a wobbly plank, tilt a spotlight, vanish again. Once he had offered her a piece of dried apple. “Good for nerves,” he had rumbled, like earth after a tremor. She had taken it gratefully, the sweet chew a small comfort against perfection’s looming pressure. He always seemed to know when a quiet word or sawdust-scented peace was required.

Dusk brought the real trouble. The main stage waited for Bartholomew Buttonwick, legendary storyteller, whose voice could make a barge listen, and for a grand entrance banner. Master Hemlock had commissioned a reproduction of Oakhaven’s first charter: faded gold thread, eloquent script, settlers and river trade stitched as if the canal itself had signed. Beautiful. Impossibly heavy. Designed to be admired in a museum light, not walked across a festival green by mortals or even a team of very strong moles. When the crew tried to lift it, the sturdy poles groaned and the fabric sagged as if centuries had sat down in the weave and refused to stand for a curtain call.

Cora’s heart leaped. A practical problem Elara, queen of finish, might miss. She scurried backstage inventing lighter cloth, folding tricks, discreet counterweights in the flats. She pictured presenting a useful banner while Elara still frowned at the original.

Elara was already there, wings neat, hawk-calm. Before Cora could speak, the swan produced a sketch: not a replacement banner, but a system of counterweights and pulleys a child could hoist. Brilliant. Elegant. Diagrams fit for an engineer’s guild.

Cora sank onto a hay bale. Elara’s competence was a tide. “I asked for subtlety and received a banner that requires bridge builders,” she muttered, tasting sawdust. Elara, with a few gestures and a quiet word, had already begun organising helpers. Seamless. So Elara.

Ned emerged from discarded scripts, wiping his brow. “Quite the banner. Never seen the like at a book festival.”

Cora kicked a pebble. “Too much. And she is so good it is impossible to be properly irritated. I wanted to fix something, not be outshone by a solution so perfect it is no longer a problem.”

Ned coiled discarded rope, paws quick. “Master Hemlock wanted a banner hung before the guest arrives. Grand, yes. Hung, more yes. Art that stays in the studio does not impress a crowd. I have seen magnificent contraptions tangle in their own cleverness.”

Steam rose. Last sun caught the dust. They sat among props with paper cups of lukewarm tea while festival murmur drifted in. Cora looked at the gleaming web of Elara’s ropes, at the historical deadweight, at Ned unspooling more line.

A thought sparked. “The charter matters. Bartholomew’s reading matters more to the hour. What if we used her ingenuity for our needs? We do not have to hoist the entire document.”

Ned nodded, slow. “Take the spirit. Adapt it. We cannot hang that whole history without a crane and a backstage incident. A representation: lighter, manageable, her pulleys without the marvel becoming the show.” He gestured at the original. “Too much fabric for a quick reveal. An embroidered panel. Symbolic. Achievable. Spectacular enough.”

So they worked through the last of the tea and the first of the lantern-lighting. Ned made the impossible simple: a shorter run of rope, a kinder hitch, a test pull that did not groan. Cora’s hooves took the delicate stitches. They measured twice, cut a lighter silk that was still rich enough to look historical in lamplight, and flew gold and deep blue through only the significant passages and heraldic marks—settlers, river trade, the first honest line of the charter rather than every faded clause. Cora’s paws, so often a fraction wrong on a jacket, found their tempo in the larger cloth. Ned hummed. Sawdust sweetened the air. The new banner could flutter. It could rise on Elara’s system in moments, smooth as a well-pulled seam, without asking the stage to become a bridge.

Lanterns came on, warm gold over last-minute chaos: a missing music stand, a child practising a bow, the smell of chestnuts wandering in from the towpath. Cora watched their banner climb and billow against evening, a marriage of form and function, the charter’s spirit without the charter’s tonnage. Elara passed, unhurried among the flats, and paused. Her keen eyes took it in—the silk, the hitch, the way the gold thread caught. Then, rare as a perfect French seam on the first try, she gave a small appreciative nod.

Cora felt a warmth that was not victory over a rival. They had not stopped Elara from being good. They had learned to be useful in their own stitches: her design, their weight, the festival’s clock. Bartholomew Buttonwick’s voice rolled across the grounds and the crowd answered. The original charter stayed where heavy things belong. The silk went up. Ned offered another sliver of dried apple, and Cora, for once, did not drop a stitch while taking it.

And if a swan’s pulley and a deer’s needle can share a sky, why then, the charter was never the only document that needed a lighter draft.
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
